frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons and export infrastructure, but European buyers seek pricing flexibility and diversified supply. Long-term dependence on gas revenues remains a structural vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Libya, and Niger increases border-security costs and complicates Algeria's non-interventionist regional posture. External military and political competition around the Sahel adds pressure.

frictionVectors.title: External control of hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Angola has strengthened state oversight and pursued diversification, but foreign operators, oil-service firms, and external finance remain central to production. Debt service and declining mature fields constrain policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The corridor is attracting United States, European, and Chinese interest because of its access to Central African minerals. Infrastructure investment can improve sovereignty while also creating competing external dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Niger pipeline and border tensions
frictionVectors.details: Benin's role in exporting Nigerien crude has become entangled with political and border disputes. The episode exposes dependence on cross-border infrastructure and the vulnerability of trade sovereignty to regional regimes.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity from the Sahel is increasing demands on border surveillance and transport infrastructure. Benin is balancing security cooperation with outside partners against concerns about operational dependence.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana continues pressing for greater local value capture, diamond marketing power, and beneficiation. Its negotiating strength is significant, but the economy remains exposed to global diamond demand and external expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral and power infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, coal, and other minerals could diversify exports but may reproduce enclave-style extraction. Limited domestic power and logistics capacity create openings for foreign capital to shape project terms.

highlights: Gold sovereignty is a political priority

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector nationalization drive
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking tighter control over industrial mining, local processing, and gold revenues. Production disruption, informality, and limited technical capacity could still leave room for opaque external intermediaries.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The junta's security relationship with Russia-linked actors offers an alternative to Western partnerships but risks political and commercial dependency. Persistent insurgency also threatens mining zones, roads, and state revenue collection.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Informal Mining
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked traders and opaque networks retain substantial influence over coltan, gold, and rare-mineral supply chains. Weak traceability limits Burundi's ability to capture value or enforce sovereign oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border and Security Friction
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over armed-group accusations and border security. Disruptions risk constraining trade routes and increasing dependence on alternative regional partners.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Ports and Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Port, shipping, telecommunications, and digital infrastructure depend heavily on foreign capital and strategic partners. This supports connectivity but narrows Praia's room to maneuver over critical assets.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago remains vulnerable to imported fuel, desalination costs, and climate stress. Tourism revenue and donor support provide resilience but leave the economy exposed to external shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-Concession Opacity
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and mining concessions remain dominated by state-linked and foreign commercial interests, with limited public transparency. Fiscal pressure increases incentives to expand extraction without strengthening local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Kribi Infrastructure and Regional Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Kribi deep-water port and associated corridors are strategically important to foreign investors and neighboring landlocked states. Dependence on external financing and operators creates leverage over Cameroon’s trade and logistics priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Russian Influence
frictionVectors.details: Security cooperation with Russian-linked forces has strengthened regime protection while deepening outside influence over gold and diamond zones. State control over production, taxation, and export channels remains weak.

frictionVectors.title: Bangui-Douala Supply Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies on a vulnerable foreign transit corridor for fuel, food, and manufactured goods. Insecurity and poor roads allow neighboring states, armed groups, and external contractors to shape access to strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Dependence and Foreign Operators
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenue remains concentrated within the central state and exposed to foreign technical and commercial partners. Limited diversification and opaque revenue management weaken broad-based national control of resource wealth.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Chad's strategic position near Sudan, Libya, and the Central African Republic gives foreign powers continued interest in its bases, intelligence access, and security partnerships. This bargaining power protects the regime but constrains fully autonomous foreign and infrastructure policy.

highlights: Mayotte dispute remains central to national sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE SOVEREIGNTY DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to claim Mayotte, while France maintains administrative control and security ties there. The dispute limits diplomatic normalization and fuels domestic political pressure.

frictionVectors.title: DEPENDENCE ON EXTERNAL CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and public services rely heavily on French, Gulf, and multilateral support. Limited domestic fiscal capacity constrains Comoros's ability to set independent development priorities.

highlights: Critical minerals remain exposed to external capture

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACTS AND CRITICAL MINERALS
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains strategically important but is shaped by foreign operators, opaque contracting concerns, and weak local value addition. Kinshasa is seeking stronger bargaining power and more domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN CONFLICT AND REGIONAL INTERVENTION
frictionVectors.details: Armed-group violence and tensions involving Rwanda continue to undermine territorial sovereignty in the east. Regional diplomacy and external security assistance have not yet produced durable control or civilian protection.

highlights: Oil revenues anchor a centralized state
Chinese infrastructure ties deepen strategic dependence

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The economy and public finances remain highly exposed to oil production, prices, and foreign technical and commercial partners. Limited diversification reduces sovereign leverage over resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: CHINA-LINKED INFRASTRUCTURE AND DEBT
frictionVectors.details: Chinese involvement in roads, telecommunications, and extractive activity provides essential capital but can narrow procurement and policy autonomy. Debt-management pressures remain a constraint on bargaining power.

highlights: Regional economic hub expands domestic leverage

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has strengthened producer-oriented regulation and is pursuing greater local processing, but multinational buyers and volatile global prices still capture substantial value. Climate stress adds pressure to the sector.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND INFRASTRUCTURE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and transport expansion is improving national and regional connectivity, while Chinese, European, and Gulf-linked firms compete for major projects. The government retains comparatively strong negotiating capacity.

highlights: Strategic ports convert geography into state revenue

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN MILITARY PRESENCE
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities provide revenue and security but make Djibouti vulnerable to great-power competition. Balancing these relationships is central to national sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, DEBT, AND LOGISTICS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's economy depends heavily on port services and Ethiopian trade, with major infrastructure ties to China and other external investors. Debt exposure and limited domestic production reduce the state's room for independent economic strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Suez and Red Sea disruption
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and rerouting around the Red Sea continue to threaten Suez Canal revenues and Egypt's foreign-exchange position. Cairo is balancing maritime security cooperation with efforts to preserve independent control over the canal corridor.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF support and Gulf investment provide liquidity but increase outside influence over state assets, exchange-rate policy, and major infrastructure. Debt servicing constrains Cairo's ability to retain full strategic discretion over development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas revenue erosion
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and limited diversification are reducing the state's control over future fiscal resources. Foreign operators retain substantial technical and capital leverage as Malabo seeks to extend production and develop gas assets.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and energy infrastructure remain important to the country's development model. This provides capacity but can deepen repayment, contracting, and strategic dependence on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb give Asmara leverage amid regional naval competition and the Sudan and Ethiopia crises. External security interest raises bargaining power but also increases pressure over port access and alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Gold and other mineral projects depend heavily on foreign capital, technology, and operating expertise. Limited transparency and sanctions-related constraints make it difficult for the state to capture stable, broad-based value from extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Regional economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's trade, power connections, logistics, and investment remain closely tied to South Africa and the Southern African Customs Union. This supports stability but limits independent control over supply chains and fiscal policy.

frictionVectors.title: Political legitimacy and investment risk
frictionVectors.details: Persistent political tensions can deter diversified investment and leave the kingdom reliant on established external commercial networks. Infrastructure and industrial projects therefore remain vulnerable to regional market conditions and donor preferences.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam improves Addis Ababa's control over electricity generation and development planning, but Egypt and Sudan continue to oppose unilateral operating decisions. Disputes over filling, drought management, and data sharing remain a major regional security risk.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, foreign-exchange shortages, and reliance on external lenders constrain Ethiopia's ability to finance transport, power, and telecom infrastructure on sovereign terms. Conflict-related destruction further increases dependence on outside capital and humanitarian systems.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Processing Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: The transition authorities are seeking greater domestic value addition and state participation in manganese and iron-ore projects. Foreign operators remain essential for capital, technology, and export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: French Commercial Retrenchment
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is recalibrating long-standing French economic and security ties while courting Gulf, Asian, and regional partners. This diversification increases bargaining room but may strain established infrastructure and investment networks.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on regional corridors through Senegal and external financing for transport and energy upgrades. This limits independent control over trade routes and raises sensitivity to bilateral tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal Land and Fisheries Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and weak monitoring continue to challenge sovereign control over marine resources. Coastal development and tourism investment also create recurring disputes over land access and environmental safeguards.

highlights: Gold and Oil Value Capture Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Mining Fiscal Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Accra is pressing mining companies for stronger fiscal returns, local procurement, and processing while needing foreign capital to sustain production. Illegal mining continues to damage waterways and complicate state resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Power-sector arrears and dependence on imported fuel constrain economic sovereignty. IMF-backed reforms and external lenders provide stabilization but narrow short-term room for independent spending choices.

highlights: Junta Uses Minerals to Consolidate Power

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Foreign Consortiums
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore and rail-port system is dominated by large foreign-backed consortia, especially Chinese-linked interests alongside international mining firms. Conakry seeks infrastructure and domestic-processing gains, but financing and technical dependence remain substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Political Transition and Contract Risk
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses mining concessions and export controls to reinforce legitimacy while delaying a full return to civilian rule. Uncertainty over licensing, labor rights, and local benefits raises friction with investors and neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Cashew Trade
frictionVectors.details: Cashew exports provide vital foreign exchange, but financing, storage, and processing are heavily shaped by external traders. Limited domestic processing leaves producers exposed to price swings and reduces national value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port, Fisheries, and Security Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime enforcement enables disputes over foreign fishing access and undermines control of coastal resources. Institutional fragility also leaves port infrastructure and security policy vulnerable to outside political and commercial influence.

highlights: Ports and energy remain strategic battlegrounds

frictionVectors.title: External debt and conditional finance
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and large external repayments constrain Nairobi's room to direct public investment and protect strategic assets. Chinese, Gulf, and Western lenders compete for influence over infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and port-corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and transport corridor remain exposed to commercial competition, local opposition, and insecurity. Foreign-backed logistics and energy projects can deepen connectivity while limiting Kenya's control over long-term revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water transfers to South Africa generate vital revenue but leave Lesotho dependent on South African financing, infrastructure, and purchasing power. Delays, cost overruns, and security disputes can weaken Maseru's bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and labor-market vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The garment sector remains highly exposed to foreign buyers, trade preferences, and shifting Asian supply chains. External firms capture substantial value while local fiscal and employment gains remain vulnerable to policy changes abroad.

highlights: Ports and concessions attract competing powers

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to Liberia's growth strategy, but foreign operators control capital, logistics, and market access. Concession renegotiations are politically sensitive because the state has limited alternatives for revenue and employment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure influence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and rail-linked projects draw interest from international mining, shipping, and development actors. Weak domestic infrastructure and regulatory capacity limit Liberia's ability to capture full value from strategic corridors.

highlights: Oil remains fragmented across rival authorities
Foreign patrons shape security and exports

frictionVectors.title: Divided control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed networks continue to use fields, export terminals, and budget allocations as leverage. Production stability depends on bargains among domestic factions rather than a unified sovereign energy strategy.

frictionVectors.title: External military and commercial influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked actors, Gulf states, Egypt, and European powers pursue overlapping security and energy interests. Foreign support reinforces fragmentation and can redirect oil infrastructure decisions away from nationally accountable institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, cobalt, and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects provide export earnings but leave Madagascar exposed to foreign capital, commodity prices, and disputes over taxation, land, and environmental damage. Local value addition remains limited relative to external control of technology and markets.

frictionVectors.title: Resource corridors and conservation finance
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed roads, ports, and biodiversity programs influence access to land and strategic resources. Conservation funding can support resilience, but restrictions and external oversight often generate sovereignty concerns among communities and policymakers.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium Project Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The planned restart of Kayelekera uranium mining could improve export earnings but leaves Malawi reliant on foreign capital, operators, and commodity markets. Contract transparency and domestic value capture remain sensitive issues.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and Power Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Fuel shortages, foreign-exchange constraints, and dependence on imported energy limit policy autonomy. External financing conditions continue to shape infrastructure and subsidy decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Confrontations
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is seeking a larger state share of gold revenues and tighter control over foreign miners, creating recurring disputes with international operators. Production and investment remain exposed to regulatory uncertainty and insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence on Russia
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support has reduced Western influence but increased dependence on an external military partner. Persistent jihadist violence continues to threaten transport corridors, mines, and state authority.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Project Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project with Senegal is expanding Mauritania's strategic weight, but revenue sharing, local content, and cross-border infrastructure remain politically sensitive. Foreign operators retain significant technical and financial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports and planned logistics expansion depend heavily on foreign investment, rail capacity, and external commodity demand. Nouakchott is improving bargaining power but has limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia Settlement
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to negotiations over the future of Diego Garcia and associated security arrangements. The issue tests its ability to convert diplomatic recognition into effective maritime control.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, satellite, undersea-cable, and maritime-security partnerships expose Mauritius to competing Indian, Chinese, Western, and regional interests. The government must balance investment access with protection of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy, and infrastructure projects in Western Sahara remain central to Morocco's sovereignty strategy but attract legal and diplomatic challenges from Algeria and the Polisario Front. External recognition and investor risk assessments remain decisive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is using European, Gulf, Chinese, and American capital to accelerate ports, renewables, batteries, and green hydrogen. This strengthens capacity while creating exposure to external technology, financing, and market conditions.

highlights: Cabo Delgado Insurgency Limits State Control

frictionVectors.title: LNG and Foreign Security Presence
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies retain major leverage over the Rovuma Basin, while offshore gas development depends on foreign financing and security support. Insurgent violence and local grievances continue to constrain Mozambique's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Beira, Nacala, and Maputo corridors attract competing Gulf, Chinese, South African, and Western commercial interests. The state benefits from transit investment but faces limited control over financing terms and strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Oil and Gas Windfall Under Negotiation

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Emerging Hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries have increased Namibia's leverage but also made production-sharing terms and local-content rules more contested. International oil majors and foreign investors remain essential to developing the fields.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Green Hydrogen Finance
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, and Asian partners are competing for uranium, lithium, rare-earth, and green-hydrogen opportunities. Namibia is strengthening domestic value-addition requirements, but capital and technology dependence remain substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control and renegotiation of longstanding foreign mining relationships, especially in uranium. Commercial uncertainty and deteriorating security have complicated production, exports, and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Niger's break with France and weakened ties with Western partners have opened space for Russian security cooperation. The shift may reduce Western influence but leaves the country dependent on external military suppliers while insurgent violence persists.

highlights: Oil Theft and Infrastructure Gaps Persist

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Foreign Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Dangote refinery and planned domestic gas expansion improve Nigeria's autonomy, but upstream production still relies heavily on foreign technology, financing, and joint ventures. Regulatory uncertainty continues to deter investment in mature and deepwater assets.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Security and Oil Theft
frictionVectors.details: Vandalism, crude theft, and insecurity in the Niger Delta reduce state revenue and weaken effective control over energy infrastructure. Private security networks and local political brokers remain influential around key production corridors.

highlights: Minerals Strategy Seeks Local Value Addition
Eastern Congo Tensions Raise External Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Conflict Minerals and Regional Scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role in regional mineral trading is under sustained international scrutiny because of allegations linking supply chains to conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Kigali denies supporting illicit extraction, but diplomatic and sanctions risks remain elevated.

frictionVectors.title: Security Partnerships and Strategic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda uses external security partnerships, development finance, and peacekeeping deployments to strengthen its regional position. These relationships bring resources and influence but expose Kigali to pressure from Western donors and neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore licensing uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Longstanding petroleum expectations have produced limited commercial results, leaving the country dependent on external capital and technical expertise. Any future licensing could create sovereignty concerns if contract terms are opaque.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Sao Tome and Principe relies on foreign partners and regional mechanisms to monitor its waters and protect prospective offshore assets. Limited naval capacity constrains independent enforcement of maritime rights.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign energy-sector exposure
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil and gas development offers Dakar new revenue and bargaining power, but production remains tied to international operators, financing, and technical supply chains. Contract renegotiation pressures could unsettle investors while testing national control.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Expansion around Dakar and competing regional transport corridors is drawing Gulf, European, Chinese, and Turkish commercial interest. Infrastructure financing can improve connectivity but may create long-term dependence through debt, concessions, or strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: External maritime-security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from cooperation with India, France, the United States, and other partners to monitor its vast exclusive economic zone. This improves protection against piracy and illegal fishing but limits purely autonomous control of maritime surveillance.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign ownership in tourism and fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, fisheries, and port services remain vulnerable to concentrated foreign capital and market shocks. The government is seeking greater local value capture while preserving investment needed by a small island economy.

frictionVectors.title: Large-scale mining concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, bauxite, and diamond operations provide essential foreign exchange but expose the state to commodity cycles, foreign corporate leverage, and contested revenue-sharing arrangements. Weak local processing limits domestic control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependency
frictionVectors.details: Mining exports depend on externally financed roads, ports, and logistics networks, giving investors significant influence over strategic infrastructure. Chinese, Middle Eastern, and Western commercial interests compete for access and concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource competition
frictionVectors.details: Prospective oil and gas development is entangled with federal-state disputes, maritime disagreements, weak regulatory capacity, and security risks. External firms and neighboring states may gain disproportionate influence unless licensing and revenue-sharing systems become more transparent.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic port access
frictionVectors.details: Berbera, Mogadishu, Kismayo, and other ports attract Gulf, Turkish, Chinese, and Western security and logistics interests. Foreign-backed port and military arrangements can improve infrastructure while intensifying sovereignty disputes and regional rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic beneficiation and bargaining power over platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth supply chains. Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors remain influential in processing, finance, and offtake agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and logistics vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, port congestion, and freight-rail deterioration continue to constrain sovereign control over mineral exports. Private operators and external financiers are increasingly important to infrastructure recovery.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies heavily on oil revenues and transit infrastructure through Sudan, leaving production exposed to conflict, pipeline disruption, and opaque commercial arrangements. Foreign operators and neighboring states retain substantial leverage over extraction and export access.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security influence
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and armed violence allow neighboring governments and external security actors to shape border trade, transport corridors, and elite bargaining. Weak institutions limit the state's ability to convert resource wealth into sovereign development.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and wartime finance
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling networks continue to finance competing armed actors, with foreign intermediaries and regional markets influencing access and pricing. Formal state oversight over extraction and export has sharply weakened.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: The Red Sea ports, transport corridors, and key energy infrastructure are strategically important to domestic factions and outside powers. Conflict damage and competing foreign relationships threaten national control over trade gateways and reconstruction priorities.

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining balance
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking stronger state participation, local content, and fiscal returns from planned offshore gas development. Major international energy companies and project financiers retain leverage over technology, timelines, and export terms.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral and transport concessions
frictionVectors.details: Gold, nickel, graphite, and transport-corridor projects are expanding under tighter government oversight. The central challenge is converting foreign capital and infrastructure partnerships into domestic processing and durable strategic control.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hinge

frictionVectors.title: Port-centered external dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé and its logistics ecosystem generate strategic leverage but depend heavily on foreign capital, shipping networks, and regional transit demand. Competition among external commercial and security partners shapes customs, infrastructure, and corridor priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability in the Sahel are increasing pressure on northern Togo and its transport routes. Expanded foreign security cooperation may improve protection while narrowing the government's room for independent strategic choices.

frictionVectors.title: Migration and financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: European partners retain substantial leverage through migration-control cooperation, budget support, and investment ties. This narrows Tunisian policy autonomy even as the government resists externally imposed conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and phosphate constraints
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported hydrocarbons and declining phosphate-sector performance limits fiscal and strategic room for maneuver. Renewable-energy projects offer diversification but remain reliant on foreign capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions risk
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil corridor remains central to Kampala's resource strategy but faces international environmental criticism, financing constraints, and dependence on foreign contractors and investors.

frictionVectors.title: DRC-border security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Operations and trade routes connected to eastern DRC expose Uganda to persistent security and diplomatic risks. Regional military and commercial involvement can generate influence while complicating sovereign oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using global demand for copper and cobalt to seek better investment terms and local processing, but remains dependent on multinational operators, foreign technology, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has improved fiscal credibility but constrains spending choices and increases reliance on external lenders. Power shortages and transport bottlenecks continue to weaken domestic control over mineral value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mineral value chains
frictionVectors.details: The government promotes domestic processing and tighter oversight of lithium, platinum, and gold, yet Chinese and other foreign investors retain substantial influence over capital, technology, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and sanctions constraints
frictionVectors.details: Chronic power shortages and restricted access to international finance undermine industrial sovereignty. Dependence on regional electricity imports and alternative external funding channels limits policy flexibility.
